title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: "It's very difficult for me to remember the earliest period of my existence. Everything from that time appears confused and blurred. A strange flood of sensations seized me. I saw, felt, heard, and smelled all at once. It took a long time before I learned to separate these different senses. Gradually, I remember, a stronger light pressed on my eyes, forcing me to shut them. Darkness then came over me and troubled me, but I had hardly felt it when the light poured in on me again — because, as I now suppose, I had opened my eyes. I walked and, I believe, went downward. Soon I noticed a big change in what I felt. Before, dark, solid objects had surrounded me — blocking both my touch and my sight. Now I could wander freely, with no obstacles I couldn't avoid or get past. The light grew more and more intense, and the heat wore me down. I looked for shade and found it in the forest near Ingolstadt. I lay by a brook to rest, until hunger and thirst roused me from my half-sleeping state. I ate berries hanging from trees or lying on the ground, drank from the brook, and lay down again. Sleep overcame me.

"It was dark when I woke. I felt cold and half-frightened, instinctively, at finding myself so alone. Before leaving your apartment, feeling cold, I'd covered myself with some clothes. But they weren't enough to protect me from the night dew. I was a poor, helpless, miserable wretch. I knew nothing, could tell nothing apart. Pain attacked me from all sides. I sat down and wept.

"Soon a gentle light crept across the sky and gave me a feeling of pleasure. I started up and saw a radiant form rising from among the trees — the moon. I stared at it in wonder. It moved slowly, but it lit my path. I went out again in search of berries. I was still cold when I found a large cloak under one of the trees. I wrapped myself in it and sat on the ground. No clear thoughts filled my mind. Everything was confused. I felt light and hunger and thirst and darkness. Countless sounds rang in my ears. Various smells surrounded me. The only thing I could make out was the bright moon, and I fixed my eyes on it with pleasure.

"Several days and nights passed. The moon shrank noticeably before I began to tell my sensations apart from one another. Gradually I could see the clear stream that gave me water and the trees that shaded me. I was delighted when I first realized that a pleasant sound I often heard came from the throats of the little winged animals that sometimes blocked the light from my eyes. I also began to observe more carefully the shapes around me and to sense the boundaries of the bright roof of light overhead. Sometimes I tried to imitate the birds' pleasant songs but couldn't. Sometimes I wanted to express my feelings in my own way, but the rough, inarticulate sounds that burst from me frightened me into silence.

"The moon disappeared from the night sky, then returned smaller. I was still in the forest. My senses had become distinct by this time, and my mind received new ideas every day. My eyes adjusted to the light and could perceive objects in their true forms. I could tell an insect from a plant and, gradually, one plant from another. I discovered that the sparrow made only harsh sounds, while the blackbird and thrush sang sweetly.

"One day, feeling cold, I found a fire left by some wandering beggars. I was overjoyed at its warmth. In my delight I thrust my hand into the glowing embers — and quickly pulled it out with a cry of pain. How strange, I thought, that the same thing could cause such opposite effects! I examined what the fire was made of and was pleased to find it was wood. I quickly gathered some branches, but they were wet and wouldn't burn. This frustrated me. I sat watching the fire. The wet wood I'd placed near the heat dried out and caught flame. I thought about this. By touching various branches, I figured out why. Then I busied myself collecting a large supply of wood to dry and burn. When night came, I was terrified that my fire might go out. I carefully covered it with dry wood and leaves, placed wet branches on top, then spread my cloak and lay down to sleep.

"In the morning, my first concern was the fire. I uncovered it, and a gentle breeze quickly fanned it into flame. I noticed this and made a fan of branches to revive the embers when they were nearly dead. That night I discovered fire gave light as well as heat, and that this discovery was useful for cooking — I found that some scraps left by the travelers tasted much better roasted than the raw berries I'd been gathering. So I tried cooking my food the same way, placing it on live coals. The berries were ruined by this, but the nuts and roots were greatly improved.

"Food, however, grew scarce. I often spent entire days searching in vain for a few acorns to ease the pain of hunger. When I realized this, I decided to leave my home and find a place where my basic needs could be met more easily. I was deeply sorry to lose the fire I'd stumbled on by accident, since I didn't know how to start a new one. I spent several hours seriously thinking about this problem but couldn't solve it. Wrapping myself in my cloak, I set out through the woods toward the setting sun. I walked for three days. Eventually I found open country. Heavy snow had fallen the night before. The fields were all white. The scene was bleak. My feet ached from the cold, damp ground.

"It was about seven in the morning. I longed for food and shelter. At last I spotted a small hut on a rise — probably built for some shepherd's convenience. This was new to me. I examined it curiously. Finding the door open, I entered. An old man sat inside, near a fire, preparing his breakfast. He turned when he heard me. Seeing me, he screamed loudly and fled from the hut across the fields with a speed his frail body hardly seemed capable of. His appearance — so different from anything I'd seen before — and his flight surprised me. But I was enchanted by the hut. Here, snow and rain couldn't reach me. The ground was dry. To me then it seemed as exquisite and divine a retreat as Pandæmonium, the palace of hell, seemed to the demons after their suffering in the lake of fire. I eagerly devoured the old man's breakfast — bread, cheese, milk, and wine (though I didn't like the wine). Then, overcome by tiredness, I lay down on some straw and fell asleep.

"It was noon when I woke. Drawn by the warmth of the sun shining brightly on the white ground, I decided to keep traveling. I put the remains of the breakfast in a bag I found and walked across the fields for several hours. At sunset I reached a village. How incredible it looked! The huts, the neat cottages, the grand houses each caught my admiration. The vegetables in gardens and the milk and cheese displayed in cottage windows made me hungry. I entered one of the best-looking cottages. But the moment I stepped inside, the children screamed and one of the women fainted. The whole village came out. Some people ran. Others attacked me, pelting me with stones and other objects until, badly bruised, I escaped to the open country. I fearfully took refuge in a low hovel — bare and wretched-looking compared to the houses I'd seen in the village. But this hovel was attached to a neat, pleasant-looking cottage. After my costly experience, I didn't dare enter it. My shelter was built of wood, so low I could barely sit upright. The floor was bare earth, but it was dry. Despite the wind whistling through countless cracks, it was a welcome haven from the snow and rain.

"I retreated here and lay down, glad to have found shelter — however miserable — from the weather and, even more, from human savagery. As soon as morning came, I crept from my kennel to examine the cottage next door and figure out if I could stay. My hovel stood against the back of the cottage, and its exposed sides were bordered by a pigsty and a clear pool of water. One side was open — the way I'd crept in. But now I blocked every crack through which I might be seen, using stones and wood arranged so I could move them to get in and out. All my light came through the pigsty, and it was enough.

"Having arranged my dwelling and carpeted it with clean straw, I retreated, for I saw a man in the distance and remembered too well what had happened in the village to trust myself in anyone's power. But first I'd secured food for the day — a stolen loaf of coarse bread and a cup I could use to drink more conveniently from the clean water flowing past my retreat. The floor was slightly raised, keeping it dry. Its closeness to the cottage chimney kept it reasonably warm.

"I decided to stay in this hovel until something changed my mind. It was a paradise compared to the bleak forest, the dripping branches, and the cold, damp earth. I ate my breakfast with pleasure and was about to move a plank to get some water when I heard a footstep. Looking through a small crack, I saw a young woman passing my hovel with a pail on her head. She was young and gentle-looking — unlike any peasant or farm servant I've since met. She was dressed simply in a coarse blue skirt and linen jacket. Her fair hair was braided but unadorned. She looked patient but sad. I lost sight of her, and in about fifteen minutes she returned with the pail partly filled with milk. As she walked, seemingly burdened by the weight, a young man met her. His face expressed even deeper sadness. Making a few melancholy sounds, he took the pail from her head and carried it to the cottage himself. She followed, and they disappeared. Soon the young man came out again with tools and crossed the field behind the cottage. The girl busied herself, sometimes inside the house, sometimes in the yard.

"Looking more carefully at my dwelling, I found that one of the cottage windows had once extended into it, but the panes had been filled in with wood. In one board was a tiny, almost invisible crack through which I could just see into the room. It was a small, whitewashed space, clean but nearly bare of furniture. In one corner, near a small fire, sat an old man with his head in his hands, looking utterly dejected. The young girl was tidying the room. Then she took something from a drawer — some kind of handwork — and sat beside the old man. He took up an instrument and began to play sounds sweeter than the song of the thrush or the nightingale. It was a beautiful sight, even to a wretch like me who had never seen anything beautiful before. The old man's silver hair and kind face filled me with reverence. The girl's gentle manner stirred my love. He played a sweet, mournful melody that drew tears from his companion's eyes. The old man didn't notice until she sobbed aloud. Then he uttered a few sounds, and the girl left her work and knelt at his feet. He raised her and smiled with such kindness and warmth that I felt emotions I'd never experienced — a strange mixture of pain and pleasure unlike hunger or cold, warmth or food. I pulled away from the window, unable to bear these feelings.

"Soon after, the young man returned, carrying a load of firewood on his shoulders. The girl met him at the door and helped him. She carried some of the wood inside and put it on the fire. Then the two went to a corner of the cottage, where he showed her a large loaf of bread and a piece of cheese. She seemed pleased and went into the garden for some roots and greens, which she put in water over the fire. She returned to her work while the young man went into the garden, digging and pulling up roots. After about an hour the young woman joined him, and they went inside together.

"Meanwhile, the old man had been sitting in thought. When the others appeared, he brightened. They sat down to eat. The meal was quickly finished. The young woman tidied up again. The old man walked outside in the sun for a few minutes, leaning on the young man's arm. Nothing could exceed the beauty of the contrast between these two. One was old, with silver hair and a face beaming with goodness and love. The other was young, slight, and graceful, his features perfectly formed — yet his eyes and bearing expressed the deepest sadness. The old man went back inside. The young man picked up different tools and headed across the fields.

"Night fell quickly. To my amazement, I discovered that the cottagers could extend the day using candles. I was delighted that sunset didn't end the pleasure I took in watching my human neighbors. In the evening, the young girl and the man were busy with tasks I didn't understand. The old man took up his instrument again and made the divine sounds that had enchanted me that morning. When he finished, the young man began — not playing music, but making sounds that were monotonous, unlike either the old man's instrument or birdsong. I later learned he was reading aloud, but at the time I knew nothing of words or letters.
"The family soon put out their lights and went to rest, as I guessed, for the night."
